title: Meet a System
learningIntention: I can recognise a digital system and explore it for a purpose.
teacherIntroduction: A system is something we use to do a job. A digital system has hardware — the parts we can touch — and software — the instructions inside. Today we will look at one digital system in our classroom, name a part we can touch, and use it for one job.
childActivity: Look at one classroom digital system, point to a part you can touch, and help use it for one job.
reflectionPrompt: What job did this system help us do?
movementMoment: Walk to the system, point to one part you can touch, then walk back to your place.
stoppingPoint: We stop after we have named a part we can touch and used the system for one job. We do not take photos or write anyone's name.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can point to a hardware part and say the job the class tried. Do not collect names, drawings of faces, or photos.
bestFit: A first Foundation Digital Technologies lesson, or a short unplugged session when students have no devices.

title: Show It Two Ways
learningIntention: I can show the same data as an object, a picture and a symbol.
teacherIntroduction: Data is information. We can show the same information in more than one way: as a real object, as a picture, and as a simple symbol. Today we will take one thing and show it in those three ways.
childActivity: Use one classroom object, draw a picture of it, and show a simple symbol that stands for the same thing.
reflectionPrompt: Which way of showing the data was easiest to understand, and why?
movementMoment: Hold the object up, sit to draw the picture, then stand and show the symbol.
stoppingPoint: We stop after the same data has been shown as an object, a picture and a symbol. We do not collect student names or photos.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can point to all three representations and say they show the same thing. Keep only what you need for your own records, with no names attached in this pack.
bestFit: After Meet a System, or as a short unplugged data lesson in Foundation.

title: What Is Mine to Keep?
learningIntention: I can identify some data that is personal and owned by me.
teacherIntroduction: Some information is about a person, and some of that information is theirs to keep. Today we will look at a few examples I have already prepared. We will decide together: is this personal data that someone owns, or is it not? We will not write our names, share photos of ourselves, or tell personal details.
childActivity: Listen to a teacher example, then point, use thumbs or walk to a hoop to show whether the data is personal and owned, or not personal.
reflectionPrompt: What is one kind of data that is yours to keep?
movementMoment: When the teacher reads an example, walk to the 'personal and owned' hoop or the 'not personal' hoop.
stoppingPoint: We stop after sorting a few teacher-prepared examples. No student names, photos or personal details are collected.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can point to one example of personal data and one that is not. Do not write student names or keep photos.
bestFit: A short Foundation lesson on personal data, using only teacher-prepared generic examples.

title: Parts of a System
learningIntention: I can identify a digital system and explore its components for a purpose.
teacherIntroduction: A digital system has parts, called components. Some components are hardware — the parts we can touch. Some are software — the instructions that tell the system what to do. Today we will look at one digital system, name more than one of its components, and use it for one purpose.
childActivity: Name two or more components of a classroom digital system and help use the system for one purpose.
reflectionPrompt: Which components did we need for the job we tried?
movementMoment: Take turns walking to the system and pointing to a component you named, then return to your place.
stoppingPoint: We stop after we have named at least two components and used the system for one purpose. We do not take photos or collect names.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can name two components and say the purpose the class tried. No names or photos.
bestFit: A Years 1–2 unplugged lesson after students have met the idea of a system, using one classroom device the teacher already has.

title: The Same Data, Many Ways
learningIntention: I can show the same data as pictures, symbols, numbers and words.
teacherIntroduction: The same data can be shown as a picture, a symbol, a number and a word. Today we will take one simple piece of classroom data and show it in all four ways, then say what stayed the same.
childActivity: Show one piece of classroom data as a picture, a symbol, a number and a word, then say what stayed the same.
reflectionPrompt: What stayed the same when we showed the data in four ways?
movementMoment: Four corners: walk to Picture, Symbol, Number or Word when the teacher names that way of showing the data.
stoppingPoint: We stop after the same data has been shown in four ways. We do not collect student names or photos.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can point to all four representations and say they show the same data. No names or photos.
bestFit: A Years 1–2 unplugged data lesson, useful after Show It Two Ways or as a short lesson on its own.

title: Follow the Steps
learningIntention: I can follow and describe an algorithm that has a sequence of steps, a decision and a repeat.
teacherIntroduction: An algorithm is a set of steps we can follow. Today we will follow one short algorithm together. It will have a sequence — an order of steps — a decision, and a repeat. Then we will say the steps in our own words.
childActivity: Follow a short class algorithm, then describe the order, the decision and the repeat.
reflectionPrompt: What was the decision in our algorithm, and what did we repeat?
movementMoment: Act out the algorithm with the class: walk the sequence, follow the decision, and repeat the action until the teacher says stop.
stoppingPoint: We stop after the class has followed the algorithm once and described the sequence, the decision and the repeat. We do not need devices, names or photos.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can follow the steps and later name the order, the decision or the repeat. No names or photos.
bestFit: A Years 1–2 unplugged algorithms lesson in a clear space, such as the mat or the playground line.

title: A Problem for Someone We Know
learningIntention: I can investigate a simple problem for a known user that a digital system could help with, and talk about whether an existing system would meet that need.
teacherIntroduction: A known user is someone we can describe by their job or role, not by writing a student's name. Today we will look at one simple problem for a known user in our school, and talk about whether an existing digital system would help. We will not use real student names or photos.
childActivity: Investigate one simple problem for a known user, then talk about whether an existing digital system would meet that need.
reflectionPrompt: Would the system we talked about meet the user's need? Why, or why not?
movementMoment: Thumbs up, sideways or down to show whether the existing system would meet the need, then stand if you can say one reason.
stoppingPoint: We stop after investigating one problem and discussing one existing system. We do not collect names, photos or personal details.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can say who the user is, what the problem is, and whether the existing system would help. No names or photos.
bestFit: A Years 1–2 unplugged lesson late in the starter set, after students can name a digital system and a purpose.
